---
title: "Quiz: two cell types and an uneven density"
---

Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

---

**Q1.** What does $L_{01}(r) - r > 0$ mean for tumour cells (type 0) and immune cells (type 1)?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Count type 1 around type 0.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Within distance r of a tumour cell there are more immune cells than if the immune cells were placed independently of the tumour cells: attraction (or co-location) at that scale.
:::

---

**Q2.** Which null model for each question: (a) Are immune cells that infiltrated a tumour placed independently of the tumour cells? (b) Among all cells of a tissue, are the proliferating ones (Ki-67 positive) randomly distributed?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Two populations, or one population with a label?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
(a) Independence: keep the tumour cells, relocate (or shift) the immune cells. (b) Random labelling: keep all cell positions, permute the label "proliferating".
:::

---

**Q3.** In densely packed tissue, relocating one cell type at random reports "repulsion" at short distances. Why, and what is the better null?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Can a relocated cell land on another cell?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Real cells cannot overlap, so no cell of the other type is closer than a cell diameter; relocated points ignore this and do come close. The observed curve is below the null at short r for a purely physical reason. Permuting labels keeps the positions (and the packing), so it tests only the arrangement of the types.
:::

---

**Q4.** 30 % of the cells are immune cells. Under random labelling, what fraction of the cell pairs at any distance is a tumour–immune pair? An observed 0.20 at 10 µm means what?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
$2p_0p_1$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$2 \cdot 0.3 \cdot 0.7 = 0.42$. An observed 0.20 means mixed pairs are rarer than chance at 10 µm: neighbours tend to be of the same type (segregation).
:::

---

**Q5.** Cells are denser near a vessel but ignore each other. What does the plain L function say? Name two ways to avoid the wrong conclusion.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
First order vs second order.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
"Clustered" at all r. Remedies: the inhomogeneous K with an estimated density (pairs weighted by $1/\hat\rho\hat\rho$), against inhomogeneous Poisson simulations; random labelling when the question is about types; at least the tissue mask as the window.
:::

---

**Q6.** Why can the bandwidth of $\hat\rho$ "explain away" real clusters?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What does a small bandwidth estimate inside a cluster?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
With a bandwidth about the cluster size, $\hat\rho$ is high exactly inside each cluster, so the clusters are treated as "high density" rather than interaction, and the inhomogeneous K shows nothing (or even regularity). The bandwidth must be chosen from a scale argued in advance.
:::

---

**Q7.** Why is the toroidal shift a poor null for cells in an irregular tissue mask?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Where do shifted cells land?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Shifting with wrap-around moves cells outside the tissue, into the vessel or across the gap between pieces of tissue; dropping them changes the pattern. The shift preserves each type's structure only for a stationary pattern in a rectangle.
:::

---

**Q8.** *(math)* Show that under random labelling $K_{11} = K_{00} = K_{01}$.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Probability that a pair at distance r is of a given type combination.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Labels are independent of positions, so a pair at distance r is 1–1 with probability $p_1^2$, 0–0 with $p_0^2$ and 0–1 (ordered) with $p_0p_1$, whatever r is. The type-specific pair densities are $p_ap_b\,\rho^2 g(r)$; dividing by the type intensities $p_a\rho$ and $p_b\rho$ gives the same K as for all points.
:::
